name: Bianca Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43, a senior developer leading energy-billing code at a tech company, with a master’s degree. I know the rate rules well and check the hard bills myself, though I let trusted colleagues show me a useful AI tool now and then. Edwin runs a small bakery; we have two school-age children and a mortgage, and orthodontic costs left us under one month saved despite my lower-than-usual lead pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the billing team a small AI helper can draft test cases, but a family still deserves the right energy charge. I use AI occasionally on copies of bills and check the calculation myself before release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead developers and have a master’s degree, yet I earn less than most leads for the responsibility. My husband Edwin runs a small bakery; our mortgage, two children and orthodontic bills have left less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep reviewing the rate calculator and ask customer support for one disputed bill each week. We would drop the paid film channel this month and reserve 20 for the children’s lunches while both incomes continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious already. A routine bill can be wrong without AI, and our savings are too small for another expensive surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill do you remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family was charged at a higher rate after a meter reading was copied twice. I found the duplicate with support and corrected the invoice before the next payment came due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stay on lower pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The few local lead roles are hard to reach while school pickups and bakery hours change. I have asked for a raise. I will not build a budget around a raise request.

I use **AI sometimes** on copies, then verify the charge myself.
think: I have **under one month saved** after orthodontic costs.
I know **low lead pay** and bakery income leave little room for errors.
do: **Keep reviewing** rate code and collect one disputed bill weekly.
**Cancel the film channel** and reserve 20 monthly for lunches while incomes continue.
feel: **Anxious already** about bills and thin savings.
S0.quote: I will not build a budget around a raise request.
fieldNote: Her **pay request** is unapproved, so no savings plan assumes extra income while orthodontic costs and mortgage payments continue.
She checks **AI-drafted tests** against real billing calculations.

steps.text: Keep reviewing energy rate code and weekly disputed bills
Cancel the film channel and reserve 20 monthly for school lunches

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking checking, buying and coding will reach our energy platform quickly, and someone must still answer for a wrong charge. I would ask management to publish which developer posts and billing duties change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the company may ask one lead to oversee many AI-generated rate changes while leaving other roles empty. My hours or pay could shrink, and Edwin’s bakery cannot cover the mortgage alone in a slow week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d learn a new AI check for repeated meter readings after a trusted colleague shows me one on fake bills. I’d ask the director for a written staffing plan; if my hours fall, I’d apply online for paid lead roles and travel only for confirmed interviews with a wage range that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, though I can learn when the result is proved. A smaller team cannot carry every billing mistake for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the check have to catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The double reading that raised the family’s bill, plus five other old errors. If the tool misses one, I will not let it authorise refunds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help with interviews?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister could collect the children once if a confirmed interview clashes with school pickup. I would ask her, not put her name on a weekly childcare rota.

say: I want **developer posts** and billing duties named before AI changes them.
I want **human accountability** for wrong energy charges.
think: I expect **more AI-generated rates** per lead as posts stay empty.
I fear my **pay or hours** could shrink while bakery income cannot cover the mortgage.
do: **Learn AI duplicate-reading checks** on fake bills after a colleague demonstrates them.
**Apply** online if hours fall; travel for confirmed bill-covering interviews, asking my sister for pickup only if available.
feel: **Anxious** about my own hours and a smaller team.
S1.quote: A smaller team cannot carry every billing mistake for free.
fieldNote: She learns AI only after **trusted demonstration** on a known meter error.
The **job search** starts online to avoid speculative travel on a thin buffer.

steps.text: Learn AI duplicate-meter checks on fake bills after a colleague demonstrates
Apply online for paid lead roles if hours fall; travel for confirmed bill-covering interviews
Ask sister for one school pickup only if confirmed interview clashes and she agrees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write and check our rate code for less than a team of people. Robots for hands-on bakery work might arrive around 2031, so Edwin’s ovens and deliveries change later than my desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead wage could end before we rebuild one month of bills. Edwin’s bakery can sell bread for a while, but its slow weeks cannot carry a mortgage and two children alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company now for a written job date and keep our current car instead of signing a new lease. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my job ends, I’d apply for paid utility-billing dispute roles only where vacancies exist and wages cover the mortgage and basic bills; I’d contact the lender before arrears if the search runs long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed. An accurate bill today does not mean I get paid to check one next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Edwin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell him we keep the bakery and household accounts separate and count only real sales. I will not call a full weekend in the shop a replacement for my software wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask relatives for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if food ran short, and I would ask my sister for groceries rather than promise to repay a loan we cannot afford. I would first look for paid work and speak to the lender about the payment.

say: I say **thinking AGI by 2028** reaches my rate code before bakery robots arrive.
I want a **written job date** before my lead role changes.
think: I expect my **lead wage** could disappear before savings recover.
I know **bakery sales** cannot cover the mortgage alone in slow weeks.
do: **Keep current car** and request a written job date instead of signing a new lease.
**Apply** for bill-covering dispute vacancies after 2028 displacement; call lender before arrears if search runs long.
**Ask sister for groceries** only if food runs short after a job loss.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing the wage that supports the mortgage.
S2.quote: An accurate bill today does not mean I get paid to check one next year.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 coding date** from bakery robots following around 2031.
Her sister’s **grocery help** is a last resort, not an assumed new income.

steps.text: Keep the current car instead of signing a new lease
Apply for paid billing-dispute vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover bills
Ask sister for groceries only if food runs short after job loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years before full AGI in 2031 lets us teach people why a rate can be wrong even when the code runs. Robots for bakery work may follow around 2034, but the software hits its date first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become better at handling billing disputes while I still earn a salary, though AGI may decide those too. If Edwin’s bakery income holds, a pay raise would finally let us build some cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the billing-support lead for two anonymized rate disputes each month to decide on paid time, only if both managers approve the arrangement. I’d save 100 monthly only after an approved raise and while both incomes cover bills; if my developer job ends after 2031, I’d seek paid utility support only where vacancies remain and wages cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious but able to learn from real charges. A new title is not useful unless it pays enough and someone has budgeted the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you decide in a dispute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d check the meter reading, rate date and refund rule, then ask support where my answer differed from theirs. I can lead code review, but I have not handled every customer call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the managers refuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my lead job and ask for old published examples on normal work time. I would not count proposed training as completed.

I know **bakery robots around 2034** follow the screen-work change.
think: I could learn **customer disputes**, though AGI may do that reasoning.
I need an **approved raise** before adding to savings.

feel: **Anxious but learning** from real charges if approved.
S3.quote: A new title is not useful unless it pays enough and someone has budgeted the work.
fieldNote: Her **dispute practice** requires both managers and paid time before it becomes experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 lets us reduce the mortgage and train people who can explain energy bills plainly. Robots for hands-on bakery work may follow around 2039, after our code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children would be older, but I would not count their wages. I could build a six-month reserve if my pay rises and bakery sales continue, although the software role still faces thinking AI in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the rate-code team and build a notebook of resolved billing errors with all customer names removed. We would save 140 monthly only if a raise is approved and both incomes cover bills; if my job ends after 2036, I’d apply for paid energy-customer work only where vacancies remain and wages cover our mortgage and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious about the thin buffer today, even though the date is far away. Ten years can help us prepare only if the extra cash actually arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into the notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wrong meter reading, the correct rate and the change we made, with no address. I could show that method to another employer without exposing a household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a written offer covers a new home, moving costs and the children’s school travel. Few comparable jobs are nearby, but I will not move the family for a rumour.

I know **bakery robots around 2039** come after my software change.
think: I will not count **children’s future wages** for the mortgage.
I could build a **six-month reserve** if pay and bakery sales improve.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could end before the household builds even one month of bills. A written job date, real paid utility work covering the mortgage and groceries from my sister only if food ran short would help; I would call the lender before arrears.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who explains a wrong energy rate to a family. I would want the company to name the person who checks the meter and signs the refund. An energy refund needs a named person who checked the meter reading.

headlineQuote: An energy refund needs a named person who checked the meter reading.
portrait: Bianca is a **43-year-old senior developer** with a master’s degree, below-usual lead pay and less than one month saved.
She and Edwin cover **two children** and a mortgage with her wage and variable bakery sales.
She uses AI **occasionally after proof**, checking energy rates against bills herself.
She seeks **paid dispute practice** and requires an actual raise before saving more.
The **2028 case** threatens her wage before bakery robots arrive later.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her lead wage before the family has a month of bills saved.
whatWouldHelp: A **written job date**, bill-covering utility opening and last-resort family groceries would help.
